claims.claim: Online age-checking machinery creates an answer that can be requested repeatedly.
Websites, platforms, payment firms, and governments can request an age-checking answer previously created for another interaction.
Reusing an age credential already in circulation is cheaper than conducting a fresh, isolated age check.
Services seeking the same assurance will reuse credentials already in circulation rather than perform fresh checks.
Age credentials tend to acquire non-age functions soon after entering circulation.
Each additional use of an age credential makes refusing that credential more costly.
Expanded age-credential use causes access to depend on an age-status assertion remaining attached to a person's activities.
A verifier gains value when more access points accept its credential.
A gatekeeper saves money by reusing a familiar identity or age check.
An authority gains leverage when access decisions can be audited through a single layer.
When participants choose the easiest available direction, aligned incentives drive an age-checking system toward broader identity infrastructure.
When use of a credential becomes customary, consent to present it ceases to be meaningfully voluntary.
People who decline a customary credential may be denied access to stores, forums, classrooms, or services.
In shared credential systems, a breach can adversely affect a person across multiple access points rather than only one.
In shared credential systems, a mistaken denial can follow a person across multiple access points.
Policy promises governing age-checking systems can be withdrawn or cease to constrain later conduct.
Identifiers used in age-checking systems can persist after the policies intended to constrain them have changed or disappeared.
